春秋示官人之法，有不以父故廢者，有不以世故疑者，蓋任官惟賢也。則夫歸父蓋父之愆，昭子濟父之美，春秋得不備書之以示法哉？且夫譏世官者，春秋法也。今而奔齊之歸父乃嗣興於仲遂，而返魯之昭子寔繼作於叔孫，春秋又胡爲而美之耶？蓋遂之臣於文也，如齊一行，倚强援而子惡弑，恣逆謀而出姜歸，天下之惡莫大矣。使歸父而亦遂仍焉，世官之害其曷窮乎？而父則謀國以忠，雖家遣而志弗亂；復使以禮，雖君薨而節愈明，可謂克蓋乎遂之愆者矣。故經於遂出則書，父還則書，若曰：遂之惡誠可誅也，而父之賢誰能廢之？是故崇伯殛而禹興，蔡
translation_en:
Chen Ru

Comment by Associate Examiner Qian, School Instructor: The topic is straightforward. Writers often explain at length how the Sage did not leave people’s good qualities unacknowledged, yet fall well short of elucidating the principle of impartial selection for office. This composition grasps it, and is therefore recorded as a model.

Comment by Examiner Ouyang, Librarian of the Heir Apparent: This writer excels at arranging words and juxtaposing events.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Left Admonisher: The meaning of the commentary is brought out very clearly.

The Spring and Autumn Annals sets forth principles for appointing men to office: some are not rejected because of their fathers, and some are not distrusted because they hold hereditary office. This is because appointments should be based solely on worthiness. Thus, Guifu made amends for his father’s faults, while Zhaozi furthered his father’s virtues. Could the Spring and Autumn Annals fail to record both fully, to set forth these principles? Now, censuring hereditary office is a principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals. Yet Guifu, who fled to Qi, succeeded Zhong Sui, while Zhaozi, who returned to Lu, indeed succeeded Shusun. Why, then, does the Spring and Autumn Annals praise them?

When Sui served Duke Wen, his single mission to Qi secured powerful backing, and the prince E was murdered; his unchecked treasonous plotting caused Chu Jiang to return to her native state. No wickedness in the world could be greater. Had Guifu likewise followed in Sui’s footsteps, how could the harm of hereditary office ever have ended? Yet Guifu planned for the state with loyalty: although his household was expelled, his resolve remained unshaken. He reported back from his mission according to ritual: although his lord had died, his integrity shone all the more clearly. He may be said to have made amends for Sui’s faults. Thus the Classic records Sui’s departure and also records Guifu’s return, as though saying: Sui’s wickedness certainly deserved punishment, but who could on that account reject the worthy Guifu? Thus the Earl of Chong was executed, yet Yu rose to office; Cai…

text:
叔囚而仲命昔之不以父故廢者盖如此此義
行則公選以明而植黨之私庶其用沮矣至若
豹之臣於昭也取鄆一執秉直節以衛弱君仗
忠言而紓外患魯國之良莫尚矣使昭子而弗
豹若焉世官之敗其能免乎而舍則以禮立身
不屈志於強國以忠事主不阿意於權臣可謂
克濟乎豹之美者矣故經於豹執則書舍至則
書若曰豹之良誠可任也而舍之賢人其舍諸
是故丁公世美而典兵伊陟象賢而繼相昔之
===
不以世故疑者又如此此義行則公選益明而
延世之賞庶其用勸矣噫聖人經世之用維世
之防不亦具見哉雖然歸父昭子之賢誠可用
矣然昭子之執非意如之私乎歸父之遣非季
氏之讒乎詩曰讒人罔極交亂四國成昭又何
為而莫之察乎盖魯之權在二氏也久矣揚州
之孫其及也固宜此中庸之貴去讒而大學之
貴好賢有以也夫
公會晋侯宋公衛侯曹伯莒子邾子齊世

叔囚而仲命，昔之不以父故廢者，盖如此。此義行，則公選以明，而植黨之私庶其用沮矣。至若豹之臣於昭也，取鄆一執，秉直節以衛弱君，仗忠言而紓外患，魯國之良莫尚矣。使昭子而弗豹若焉，世官之敗其能免乎？而舍則以禮立身，不屈志於強國；以忠事主，不阿意於權臣，可謂克濟乎豹之美者矣。故經於豹執則書，舍至則書，若曰：「豹之良誠可任也，而舍之賢，人其舍諸？」是故丁公世美而典兵，伊陟象賢而繼相，昔之不以世故疑者，又如此。此義行，則公選益明，而延世之賞庶其用勸矣。噫！聖人經世之用、維世之防，不亦具見哉？雖然，歸父、昭子之賢誠可用矣，然昭子之執非意如之私乎？歸父之遣非季氏之讒乎？《詩》曰：「讒人罔極，交亂四國。」成、昭又何為而莫之察乎？盖魯之權在二氏也久矣，揚州之孫，其及也固宜。此《中庸》之貴去讒，而《大學》之貴好賢，有以也夫！

公會晋侯、宋公、衛侯、曹伯、莒子、邾子、齊世
translation_en:
…Shu was imprisoned, yet Zhong received an appointment. Such were the precedents for not excluding a man on account of his father. If this principle prevails, impartial selection will become clear, and the private pursuit of factional interests may thereby be checked. As for Bao’s service to Duke Zhao, in the affair of taking Yun and the ensuing detention [?], he upheld an unwavering integrity to protect his weak ruler, and relied on loyal counsel to relieve dangers from abroad. None among Lu’s worthy servants surpassed him. Had Zhaozi failed to follow Bao’s example, could the evils of hereditary office have been avoided? Yet She established himself through ritual propriety, refusing to bend his resolve before a powerful state; he served his lord loyally, refusing to accommodate the wishes of powerful ministers. He may be said to have carried forward Bao’s virtues. Thus the Classic records Bao’s detention and also records She’s arrival, as if to say: “Bao’s goodness certainly deserved trust; could anyone discard a worthy man such as She?” Thus Duke Ding perpetuated his family’s virtues and commanded the troops, while Yi Zhi emulated his worthy father and succeeded him as chief minister. Such, again, were the precedents for not distrusting a man on account of hereditary succession. If this principle prevails, impartial selection will become still clearer, and rewards extending to successive generations may thereby encourage virtue.

Ah! Are not the sage’s means of ordering the world and his safeguards for preserving it both fully manifest here? Nevertheless, although the worthiness of Guifu and Zhaozi certainly fitted them for service, was Zhaozi’s detention not due to Yiru’s private interests? Was Guifu’s expulsion not due to the Ji lineage’s slander? The Book of Odes says: “Slanderers know no bounds; together they throw the four states into disorder.” Why, then, did Dukes Cheng and Zhao fail to perceive this? Power in Lu had long rested with the two lineages. That the flight to Yangzhou [?] should have come to pass was surely to be expected. There is good reason, then, that the Doctrine of the Mean values banishing slander and the Great Learning values loving the worthy!

The duke met with the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, and the heir apparent of Qi…

…yet did not fight. Next, the army encamped at Beilin; Chu wished to fight but could not. Then it encamped at Zheng’s eastern gate, whereupon Zheng submitted and Chu too was humbled. At that time, who did not say, “Such was Duke Dao’s ability to subdue Chu! Such was his ability to subdue Chu and thereby bring Zheng to submission!” They did not understand that his plan for giving the people respite came from Wei Jiang. Thus the state had no resources left idle, and the duke reserved no sources of profit for himself, enabling him to overcome extreme peril through thoroughly sound governance. His plan for skillful military deployment came from Zhi Ying: he divided the four armies into three forces to meet the approaching enemy, thereby breaking the enemy’s offensive vigor just as it was rising. In giving respite, he first made himself invincible and awaited an opportunity to defeat the enemy. Was this not what is called skillfully nurturing one’s material resources? In deploying his forces, he always compelled others to reveal their dispositions without revealing his own. Was this not what is called skillfully nurturing one’s courage? Thus, although the enemy pressed us hard, they assembled three times and were frustrated three times, finally losing their strength and yielding to us. Although we seemed timid in confronting them, we campaigned three times and held our positions three times, finally gaining strength and striking fear into them.

Had Wei Jiang and Zhi Ying lacked the loyalty to devise plans for their state, and had Duke Dao of Jin lacked the ability to use those plans well, when would the struggle between the Yi and the Xia—the foreign peoples and the Chinese—ever have ended? The Spring and Autumn Annals records these events in detail without abridgment, as if to say, “If among the feudal lords there is one who repels the Yi and Di and brings peace to the central states as Duke Dao of Jin did, it is permissible to accord him approval.” Yet the contest between Jin and Chu was one and the same affair: why, then, did the Sage apportion approval and disapproval in this way? Because the encroachment of a foreign ruler who usurped the title of king could not be allowed to grow, while the relative strength of the central states indeed hinged upon Zheng. This was surely a case in which there was no alternative. Alas! After Chu was exhausted and Zheng had submitted, arrogance and indolence arose, the reins of government passed into other hands, and an opening was left for powerful ministers to usurp sovereign authority. title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
以安定其所成是何也昭著不息而合同之化
浩乎無停機天之所以爲天也昭著不動而辨
異之質截乎有定體地之所以爲地也夫惟不
息也是以一動也而鼓萬物之出機天之道動
其盡之矣夫惟不動也是以一靜也而鼓萬物
之入機地之道靜其盡之矣知天地則知禮樂
矣故聖人者察於地之靜也而揭之以示人則
曰禮無體之序將假有體者以昭之也是雖謂
之地制亦可也明於天之動也而揭之以示人
===
則曰樂無聲之和將托有聲者以顯之也是雖
謂之天作亦可也是則禮樂之功其大有如此
豈徒强世而已哉雖然天地之動靜聖人固達
之爲禮樂矣然必聖人法天地之序而履以中
正法天地之和而樂以和平夫然後禮樂一舉
而天地將爲昭焉不然則儀節雖繁聲容雖盛
抑末矣有志於復古禮變今樂者尚知所本云
天子者與天地參故德配天地兼利萬物
與日月並明明照四海而不遺微小

punctuated:
以安定其所成。是何也？昭著不息，而合同之化浩乎無停機，天之所以爲天也；昭著不動，而辨異之質截乎有定體，地之所以爲地也。夫惟不息也，是以一動也而鼓萬物之出機，天之道，動其盡之矣。夫惟不動也，是以一靜也而鼓萬物之入機，地之道，靜其盡之矣。知天地，則知禮樂矣。故聖人者，察於地之靜也，而揭之以示人，則曰禮；無體之序，將假有體者以昭之也，是雖謂之地制亦可也。明於天之動也，而揭之以示人，則曰樂；無聲之和，將托有聲者以顯之也，是雖謂之天作亦可也。是則禮樂之功，其大有如此，豈徒强世而已哉？雖然，天地之動靜，聖人固達之爲禮樂矣，然必聖人法天地之序而履以中正，法天地之和而樂以和平，夫然後禮樂一舉，而天地將爲昭焉。不然，則儀節雖繁，聲容雖盛，抑末矣。有志於復古禮、變今樂者，尚知所本云。

天子者，與天地參，故德配天地，兼利萬物；與日月並明，明照四海，而不遺微小。
translation_en:
…thereby bringing stability to what it has brought to completion. Why is this? Manifest and unceasing, with its unifying transformations flowing vast and uninterrupted: this is what makes Heaven Heaven. Manifest and unmoving, with its substance that distinguishes things clearly possessing a fixed form: this is what makes Earth Earth. Precisely because Heaven never ceases, through movement it sets in motion the workings by which the myriad things emerge. Movement fully encompasses the Way of Heaven. Precisely because Earth does not move, through stillness it sets in motion the workings by which the myriad things return within. Stillness fully encompasses the Way of Earth. To understand Heaven and Earth is therefore to understand ritual and music. Thus the sage discerns Earth's stillness and holds it forth for people to see, calling it ritual. Order without form must borrow what has form to make itself manifest; it may therefore also be called something instituted by Earth. He understands Heaven's movement and holds it forth for people to see, calling it music. Harmony without sound must entrust itself to what has sound to become apparent; it may therefore also be called something created by Heaven. Such is the greatness of the efficacy of ritual and music: could they merely serve to compel the world [?]? Nevertheless, although the sage has indeed given expression to the movement and stillness of Heaven and Earth as ritual and music, he must model himself upon their order and put it into practice with centrality and correctness, and model himself upon their harmony and express it in music with peace and concord. Only then, when ritual and music are put into effect, will Heaven and Earth be made manifest through them. Otherwise, however elaborate the ceremonies and however splendid the sounds and outward forms, these remain mere inessentials. May those who aspire to restore ancient ritual and reform present-day music understand what they must take as their foundation.

The Son of Heaven forms a triad with Heaven and Earth; hence his virtue matches Heaven and Earth, and he benefits all the myriad things. His brilliance equals that of the sun and moon: his light shines throughout the Four Seas, overlooking nothing, however minute or small.

載者無弗同民吾仁也則自親親之恩而及之

記者擬君道於造化而深賛其盛焉。夫德與明，君道莫大焉者也。自非各極其盛焉，何以參天地而並日月哉？其意盖謂法象莫大乎天地也，德之小者奚足以參之？惟天子也，大觀在上，卓乎與貞觀者而同體，則與天地乎參矣。故其德之所極，何高明也！建諸天焉，而與其覆燾者無弗同；德之所積，何博厚也！建諸地焉，而與其持載者無弗同。民吾仁也，則自親親之恩而及之，盖合萬民而在容保之中矣；物吾愛也，則自仁民之恩而推之，盖合萬物而在曲成之内矣。其參於天地固如此。著明莫大乎日月也，明之小

Comment by Associate Examiner Shu, School Instructor: The sovereign upholds the three forms of impartiality; thus his virtue matches Heaven and Earth, and his illumination equals that of the sun and moon. Writers often cut off the opening sentence from what follows, which is incorrect. The occasional writer who understands this nevertheless mostly resorts to stale expressions. This composition alone is simple, concise, and clear; therefore it has been selected for inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Ouyang, Librarian: Clear and richly flowing.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Left Admonisher: Serene and understated.

The author of the Record compares the Way of the ruler to the creative workings of nature and profoundly praises its fullness. Virtue and illumination are the greatest attributes of the ruler’s Way. Unless each attains its fullest extent, how could he form a triad with Heaven and Earth and equal the sun and moon? The meaning is, surely, that no models are greater than Heaven and Earth. How could lesser virtue suffice to stand alongside them? Only the Son of Heaven, displaying a grand example on high, stands loftily as one with those whose manifestation is constant, and thus forms a triad with Heaven and Earth. How lofty and luminous, then, is the ultimate reach of his virtue! Established in Heaven, it is wholly identical with Heaven’s sheltering embrace. How broad and substantial is his accumulated virtue! Established in Earth, it is wholly identical with Earth’s sustaining support. The people are those toward whom I exercise benevolence: extending to them the kindness with which I cherish my kin, I encompass all the people within my care and protection. Things are those toward which I exercise love: extending to them the kindness with which I treat the people benevolently, I encompass all things within a nurturing that brings each to fulfillment according to its nature. Such indeed is his participation alongside Heaven and Earth. Nothing is more radiant than the sun and moon. As for lesser illumination …

punctuated:
者，又奚足以並之？惟天子也，清明在躬，昭乎與貞明者而同體，則與日月乎並矣。故其明之所照，普四海而有融，極其深矣而志自通；照之所及，周四海而無外，研其幾矣而務自成。非惟不遺夫顯也，雖微而側陋之情，亦在所旁燭矣；非惟不遺夫大也，雖小而叢曲之故，亦在所畢察矣。其並於日月又如此。是則非造化之大，不足以擬人君；而非人君之聖，又安足以擬諸造化哉？雖然，人君旣聖矣，而其自治之功，又有不容少息者，何也？造化之誠則然也。是故在朝廷，則道仁聖禮義之序；在燕處，則聽雅頌之音。而環佩鸞和之節，又無往而不密其防焉。盖必如是，而後可以法天行之健，躋日新之盛也。嗚呼，君道其艱矣哉！
第貳場
論
極高明而道中庸
王諷
translation_en:
…how could those of lesser illumination suffice to stand alongside them? Only the Son of Heaven, embodying clarity and brightness, shines in unity with their constant light and thus stands alongside the sun and moon. Hence his illuminating wisdom reaches everywhere within the Four Seas and brings enlightenment: he plumbs the depths, and people’s intentions become clear of themselves. His light encompasses the Four Seas, leaving nothing outside: he examines the incipient signs, and affairs are accomplished of themselves. He overlooks not only nothing conspicuous; even the circumstances of the obscure and lowly fall within his all-embracing light. He overlooks not only nothing great; even the causes of small, tangled, and intricate matters come under his exhaustive scrutiny. Such, too, is how he stands alongside the sun and moon. Thus nothing short of the greatness of cosmic creation suffices as a comparison for the ruler; yet without the ruler’s sagacity, how could he be compared to cosmic creation?
Nevertheless, even once the ruler has attained sagacity, his work of governing himself cannot admit the slightest pause. Why is this? The unceasing sincerity of cosmic creation makes it so. Thus, at court he speaks of the ordered principles of benevolence, sagacity, ritual propriety, and righteousness; in his private quarters he listens to the sounds of the Elegantiae and Hymns. The measured sounds of his pendant jades and carriage bells likewise ensure that, wherever he goes, his safeguards against error remain strict. Only thus can he emulate the vigor of Heaven’s movement and attain the fullness of daily renewal. Alas, how difficult is the ruler’s Way!

“Reach the Utmost Height and Brilliance, Yet Follow the Doctrine of the Mean”

貫之道學者工夫須是動靜交養内外夾持乃
爲不偏二塲不困士子以難掲書出此正欲觀

In the second session, we did not burden candidates with difficult questions; we drew this topic from the book [?] precisely to see what they had cultivated within themselves. This composition shows genuine and penetrating understanding, and its language and spirit form a harmonious whole. Its author seems to be someone whose learning goes beyond merely repeating what he has heard. We therefore selected it.

Only someone who has accumulated learning and gained insight could have written it. As the first choice of the Southern Metropolitan Region, no one could replace you.

Comment by Examiner Ouyang, Librarian: When a discourse enters into human nature and principle, precision and sound judgment are exceptionally difficult to attain. Comment by Examiner Jiang, Left Mentor: Recently, the prose used in preparation for the examinations has favored the bizarre, while neglecting the work of personal understanding. title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
中庸而高明之用行盖至虛也而至實也至神
也而至易且簡也是之謂體用之一也聖人者
斯道之管也其存心也極其公公則上達而高
明之德崇其處事也極其順順則時措而中庸
之業廣是之謂內外之合也夫惟其內外之合
也是以其靜也以高明之心而涵中庸之實理
靜固定也其動也以中庸之事而運高明之虛
心動亦定也然其動也必主乎靜則又聖人之
所以一天下之動而立人極也故君子而弗聖
人之學也則已矣君子而學夫聖人也非內外
之交修動靜之相養則亦何以立體達用而凝
夫道也哉是故君子之為學也其靜也必敬以
直內也其動也必義以方外也敬則不為物淆
不為利疚直達天德而高明之體立矣義則擬
之而言議之而動各止其所而中庸之用行矣
故曰敬義立而德不孤德不孤而道斯凝矣甚
矣子思子之善言學也今夫心之所謂高明者
其體何如也吾嘗驗諸吾心矣其冲然虛也天

translation_en:
…the Mean, and the functioning of loftiness and illumination is put into effect. It is utterly empty yet utterly substantial, utterly spiritual yet utterly easy and simple. This is what is meant by the unity of substance and function. The sage is the conduit [?] of this Way. In preserving his mind, he carries impartiality to its utmost; through impartiality he attains higher understanding, and his lofty and luminous virtue is exalted. In handling affairs, he carries accordance with principle to its utmost; through such accordance he acts as the occasion requires, and his accomplishments in the Mean become extensive. This is what is meant by the union of the inner and the outer.

Precisely because his inner and outer are united, in stillness he embraces the substantial principles of the Mean within a lofty and luminous mind: his stillness is assuredly settled. In activity, he exercises his empty, lofty, and luminous mind through affairs governed by the Mean: his activity, too, is settled. Yet his activity must take stillness as its governing basis. This is also how the sage unifies all activity under Heaven and establishes the supreme standard for humanity. Thus, if the gentleman does not undertake to learn from the sage, there is nothing more to say. But if he does learn from the sage, how could he establish substance, give full expression to function, and consolidate the Way without cultivating the inner and outer together and allowing activity and stillness to nourish each other?

Therefore, in his learning, the gentleman must, in stillness, use reverence to straighten what is within, and, in activity, use righteousness to square what is without. Through reverence he is neither confused by things nor afflicted by considerations of profit; he attains directly to Heaven’s virtue, and the lofty and luminous substance is established. Through righteousness he deliberates before speaking and considers before acting, each finding its proper resting place, and the functioning of the Mean is put into effect. Hence it is said: “When reverence and righteousness are established, virtue is not isolated.” When virtue is not isolated, the Way is thereby consolidated.

How exceedingly well Master Zisi speaks of learning! Now, what is the substance of that which we call lofty and luminous in the mind? I have examined it in my own mind. In its limpid emptiness, it is, under Heaven, …

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
下之至一也其穆然神也天下之至不一也盖
其大則流行充塞極乎天而蟠乎地而發育乎
萬物其小則茂密宛至而貫徹乎經禮曲禮之
中莫不斂而歸之乎一心雖不離乎形也而實
不滯于形雖不外于器也而實不囿于器非天
下之至高明者孰能與於此及夫有感而通也
則其冲然者於是乎有當然之則焉其穆然者
於是乎有燦然之文焉以成天地以利萬物以
秩物軌莫不有天然自有之中無太過焉無不
===
及焉引之而不能使之高焉抑之而不能使之
卑焉此則所謂中庸之道也心之迹也體用一
原焉者也然而或不能一者人有以間之也夫
惟人有以間之也是以動靜弗定也內外弗合
也虛者塞而無有以受天下之有也神者滯而
無以妙天下之賾也而其去聖道也將益遠而
益不可幾也此君子之學所以貴於極高明而
道中庸也曰然則高明之極之也柰何曰居敬
夫欲之交於氣也為聲色為臭味盖日新而無

下之至一也；其穆然神也，天下之至不一也。盖其大，則流行充塞，極乎天而蟠乎地，而發育乎萬物；其小，則茂密宛至，而貫徹乎經禮曲禮之中，莫不斂而歸之乎一心。雖不離乎形也，而實不滯于形；雖不外于器也，而實不囿于器。非天下之至高明者，孰能與於此？及夫有感而通也，則其冲然者，於是乎有當然之則焉；其穆然者，於是乎有燦然之文焉。以成天地，以利萬物，以秩物軌，莫不有天然自有之中，無太過焉，無不及焉。引之而不能使之高焉，抑之而不能使之卑焉。此則所謂中庸之道也，心之迹也，體用一原焉者也。然而或不能一者，人有以間之也。夫惟人有以間之也，是以動靜弗定也，內外弗合也，虛者塞而無有以受天下之有也，神者滯而無以妙天下之賾也。而其去聖道也，將益遠而益不可幾也。此君子之學所以貴於極高明而道中庸也。
曰：「然則高明之極之也，柰何？」曰：「居敬。夫欲之交於氣也，為聲色，為臭味，盖日新而無
translation_en:
…the utmost unity under Heaven; in its profound spiritual efficacy, it is the utmost non-unity under Heaven [?]. In its vastness, it flows everywhere and fills all space, reaching Heaven and extending throughout Earth, fostering and nourishing the myriad things. In its minuteness, it is dense and finely articulated [?], penetrating both the general principles and the detailed observances of ritual. All of this is gathered back into the single mind. Although it does not depart from form, it is not bound by form; although it does not stand outside concrete things, it is not confined by them. What but the loftiest and most luminous thing under Heaven could partake of this? When, stirred by things, it responds to them, its emptiness then possesses the standards of what ought to be, and its profound spiritual efficacy then possesses a brilliant pattern. In bringing Heaven and Earth to fulfillment, benefiting the myriad things, and ordering the norms of things, it invariably possesses an inherent, natural mean, with neither excess nor deficiency. Pulling it upward cannot make it too high; pressing it downward cannot make it too low. This is what is called the Way of the Mean: the manifestations of the mind, whose substance and functioning have a single source. Yet when these fail to be one, it is because human interference comes between them. Precisely because human interference comes between them, activity and stillness are unsettled, and the inner and outer fail to unite. What was empty becomes obstructed and can no longer receive all that exists under Heaven; what was spiritually efficacious becomes impeded and can no longer work wondrously amid the intricacies of all things. One then departs ever farther from the Way of the sages and becomes ever less able to approach it. This is why the learning of the gentleman values reaching the utmost loftiness and luminosity while following the Way of the Mean.
Someone asks: “Then how does one reach the utmost loftiness and luminosity?” The reply is: “By abiding in reverent attentiveness. When desires interact with vital energy, they take the form of sounds and sights, smells and tastes; indeed, they arise anew each day without…”

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
窮也而氣質之性亦有非吾之所能脫去者非
居敬以節之則氣爲欲動而性獨不爲之累乎
必也存之於虛明之天愼之於隱微之地養之
於勿忘勿助之間敦艮之止也而適得吾體也
安咸之貞也而不失吾常也修之損裕之益而
致養吾內也游之乎天地而同其量觀之乎萬
物而同其適通之乎古今而同其運則吾之靜
亦定而高明之心可以常存矣曰然則中庸之
道之也又奈何曰窮理夫中之散於事也有經

有足爲吾之惑者非窮理以制之則知爲物淆

焉以致其力也井以辨義中立而不倚也巽以
行權旁行而不流也乾坤焉以知以能易簡而
不失之鑿也由是而成能天地則不過由是而
兼利萬物則不遺由是而秩叙物軌則愚夫愚
婦可知可能而聖人有所不違也盖雖酬酢萬

…without end. Moreover, there are aspects of the nature arising from our physical endowment that we cannot cast off. Unless we abide in reverent attentiveness to regulate it, our vital energy will be stirred by desires; can our nature alone remain unburdened by them? We must preserve the mind in its empty and luminous heaven, exercise care in what is hidden and subtle, and nourish it between neither forgetting it nor forcibly helping it grow. By deepening the stillness of Keeping Still (Gen), we attain our proper substance; by resting in the constancy of Influence (Xian), we retain our enduring norm. Through Decrease (Sun) we cultivate it, and through Increase (Yi) we enrich it, fully nourishing what lies within us. Let the mind roam through Heaven and Earth and share their capacity; contemplate the myriad things and share their fitting ease; comprehend antiquity and the present and share their unfolding. Then, in stillness, we too will be settled, and our lofty and luminous mind can be constantly preserved.
Someone asked, “How, then, does one follow the way of the Mean?” The reply was: “By investigating principle to the utmost. When the Mean manifests itself in affairs, there are regular standards and discretionary adaptations, constant conditions and changing circumstances. It depends on the particular situation and cannot be rigidly fixed. Moreover, errors that seem right can readily delude us. Unless we investigate principle to govern them, our understanding will be confused by things; how, then, can our conduct attain the Mean? We must choose what is good to make a beginning, and hold firmly to it to bring our efforts to fruition. Through The Well (Jing), we distinguish what is right, standing in the center without inclining to either side; through The Gentle (Xun), we exercise discretion, moving in different directions without drifting away. Through The Creative (Qian) and The Receptive (Kun), we know and act, proceeding with ease and simplicity without falling into forced contrivance. Proceeding thus to fulfill the capacities of Heaven and Earth, we do not overstep; proceeding thus to benefit all the myriad things, we leave none out; proceeding thus to arrange the proper order of things, we establish what even ordinary men and women can know and practice, and what even the sage does not depart from. For although we respond to countless changes, our lofty and luminous mind indeed operates amid them, while the private self takes no part. Then…

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
動亦定而中庸之用可以常行矣夫然則大本
立而達道行而聖人之能事畢矣顧其功豈有
外于內外交修之間哉故曰子思子之善言學
也嗚呼後子思而言學者吾惑焉老佛之言曰
吾離形也吾去智也吾以極吾高明也不知其
敝也空而不足以經世則乖異之行戾之也管
商之言曰吾程功也吾計能也吾以道吾中庸
也不知其敝也術而不足以敦化則卑汚之心
累之也且其離器求道而曰高明也是自私者
===
之爲也其遺道徇器而曰中庸也是用智者之
爲也非吾之所謂高明而中庸也吾之所謂高
明而中庸者道器無間也請以吾聖賢之學驗
之彼充詘於富貴者視富貴不勝其高也而舜
禹者則巍巍乎有天下而不與其心何高明也
然而諸難之試也四嶽九官十二牧之率也洪
水之抑也六府三事之修且和也則又不曰吾
可以藐天下而漫然不爲之所也其道中庸如
此孰非其高明之心爲之哉豈惟是哉彼隕穫

translation_en:
…even in activity there is stillness, and the Mean can constantly be put into practice. Then the great foundation is established and the universally applicable Way is put into effect, and all that the sage can accomplish is fulfilled. Yet could this achievement lie anywhere beyond the joint cultivation of the inner and the outer? Thus I say: how well Master Zisi speaks of learning!

Alas! Those who have spoken of learning after Zisi leave me perplexed. The followers of Laozi and the Buddha say: “I separate myself from bodily form; I discard knowledge; thereby I bring my loftiness and illumination to their utmost.” They do not recognize the failing of this approach: it is empty and inadequate to order the world, and their aberrant conduct consequently runs counter to it. The followers of Guan Zhong and Shang Yang say: “I assess achievements; I calculate abilities; thereby I pursue my Mean.” They do not recognize the failing of this approach: it consists of techniques inadequate to deepen moral transformation, and their base and impure minds consequently encumber it. Moreover, to separate oneself from concrete things in seeking the Way and call this loftiness and illumination is the practice of the self-serving. To abandon the Way and pursue concrete things and call this the Mean is the practice of those who employ cunning. This is not what I mean by being lofty and illuminated while following the Mean. What I mean is that there is no separation between the Way and concrete things.

Let me test this against the learning of our sages and worthies. Those who swell or shrink in response to wealth and rank regard these as unsurpassably exalted [?]. Shun and Yu, however, majestically possessed all under Heaven without becoming personally attached to it: how lofty and illuminated were their minds! Yet in being tested by difficult tasks, leading the Four Mountains, the nine officials, and the twelve regional governors, restraining the floodwaters, and bringing the Six Resources and Three Affairs into good order and harmony, they did not say, “I may look down upon the world,” and carelessly leave its affairs unattended. Such was their practice of the Mean. Which of these deeds was not accomplished by their lofty and illuminated minds? Nor was this all. Those who are distressed…

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
於貧賤者必且屈志乎貧賤矣而孔顏者方且
充然自得曰樂在其中曰不改其樂其心何高
明也至其庸德之行庸言之謹博文約禮之竭
才小試之而爲乘田爲委吏爲魯司冦大而發
其兆於爲邦無不時措之宜也其道中庸如此
亦孰非其高明之心爲之哉又豈惟是哉彼湯
武之放伐伊周之攝辟犯天下之不韙而冒爲
之人孰不曰大過之舉也而其心固高明也初
非有所爲而爲之也故其大過之行也亦卒歸
===
於中庸也不然則利天下之疑流言之謗四聖
人者亦何以自解也嗚呼是豈可以易易而言
哉彼其自治之功曰精一曰禮制心義制事曰
樂堯舜之道曰敬義夾持曰思兼曰無意必固
我曰四勿請事所以交修而互養之者盖已獨
至矣由是以言則高明之極必湛一如太虚中
庸之行必順動如天地而後可以語吾聖人大
公至順之道也不然即幾微之際少有正助之
私則應感之間亦忽不自知其墮於過不及之

punctuated:
於貧賤者，必且屈志乎貧賤矣。而孔顏者，方且充然自得，曰「樂在其中」，曰「不改其樂」，其心何高明也！至其庸德之行、庸言之謹、博文約禮之竭才，小試之而爲乘田、爲委吏、爲魯司冦，大而發其兆於爲邦，無不時措之宜也。其道中庸如此，亦孰非其高明之心爲之哉？又豈惟是哉？彼湯武之放伐、伊周之攝辟，犯天下之不韙而冒爲之，人孰不曰大過之舉也？而其心固高明也，初非有所爲而爲之也。故其大過之行也，亦卒歸於中庸也。不然，則利天下之疑、流言之謗，四聖人者亦何以自解也？
嗚呼！是豈可以易易而言哉？彼其自治之功，曰「精一」，曰「禮制心，義制事」，曰「樂堯舜之道」，曰「敬義夾持」，曰「思兼」，曰「無意必固我」，曰「四勿請事」，所以交修而互養之者，盖已獨至矣。由是以言，則高明之極，必湛一如太虚；中庸之行，必順動如天地，而後可以語吾聖人大公至順之道也。不然，即幾微之際少有正助之私，則應感之間亦忽不自知其墮於過不及之
translation_en:
…when faced with poverty and low station will surely let their aspirations be subdued by them. Yet Kongzi and Yan Hui remained inwardly fulfilled and content: one said, “Joy lies within these circumstances,” and of the other it was said, “He did not change his joy.” How lofty and luminous their minds were! As for practising everyday virtues, exercising care in everyday speech, and exerting themselves fully in broad learning and the discipline of ritual, whether in a modest trial of service—as keeper of livestock, keeper of stores, or Minister of Justice in Lu—or on a greater scale, revealing the outlines of how to govern a state, their actions were invariably appropriate to the occasion. Such was their practice of the constant mean. What part of it did not arise from their lofty and luminous minds? Nor was this all. Tang and Wu banished and attacked their rulers; Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou assumed sovereign authority. They ventured to act in defiance of what all under Heaven deemed right. Who would not call these acts of extraordinary departure from the norm? Yet their minds were indeed lofty and luminous: from the outset, they acted without any ulterior purpose. Thus even their extraordinary departures ultimately returned to the constant mean. Otherwise, how could these four sages have cleared themselves of suspicions that they sought to profit from possessing the realm, or of the slanders spread by rumor?
Alas! How could this be spoken of lightly? Their efforts at governing themselves were expressed in such teachings as “Be discerning and single-minded”; “Use ritual to regulate the mind and righteousness to regulate affairs”; “Take joy in the Way of Yao and Shun”; “Let reverent attentiveness and righteousness sustain you on either side”; “Think comprehensively” [?]; “Have no arbitrary suppositions, insistence on certainty, obstinacy, or self-centeredness”; and “I ask to put the four prohibitions into practice.” Through these means of reciprocal cultivation and mutual nourishment, they had surely already attained an excellence uniquely their own. Seen in this light, the utmost loftiness and luminosity must be clear and undivided like the Great Void, and the practice of the constant mean must move in accord with circumstances like Heaven and Earth. Only then can we speak of our sages’ Way of complete impartiality and perfect accord. Otherwise, if even at the first subtle stirrings there is the slightest selfish wish to anticipate results or force growth, then, in responding to external influences, one may suddenly and unwittingly fall into the bias of excess or deficiency…

translation_en:
…the Record of the Hall of Imperial History, which we reverently received with bows.
The Kui and Bi constellations display literary brilliance; Your Majesty’s composition gloriously illuminates the virtue of successive generations. The River Chart and the Luo Writing inaugurate the destined reign; Your Majesty’s words provide a mighty model for your ministers. We had scarcely marveled at this grand spectacle in mid-heaven when we were unexpectedly honored by its bestowal in the light of day. The honor surpasses precious jade; joy overflows among the officials. We, your servants, So-and-so and the others, in fear and rejoicing, bow our heads to the ground and knock our foreheads upon it.
We humbly reflect that Yao and Shun harmonized their virtue, and the imperial undertakings of Tang and Yu shone brightly; the plans and achievements of Kings Wen and Wu shed renewed radiance, and their kingly principles were fully realized. Viewing the rivers and mountains, we admire Yu: copies of his records were kept at Yuling. Singing the Major and Minor Odes and the Hymns, we recall Tang: records [?] remained at the palace gate-towers. We lament that the Qin fires reduced the writings to ashes, yet rejoice that Zhou’s beneficent legacy was not extinguished. In the Tianlu and Shiqu libraries, the records of the two Han dynasties were fully preserved; in the Jixian and Lizheng academies, the writings of the Tang remained. When the Zhao house of Song rose in succession, its continuation of the tradition of honoring literature flourished. Yet all these works arose in response to their times and could not necessarily transmit trustworthy accounts for all eternity. Surveying antiquity, we find this already so; in the present age, the undertaking reaches its fullest splendor.
We reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor possesses the luminous clarity of fire bestowed by Heaven and daily renews the embellishments of civilization. An auspicious name was first bestowed, and a propitious day chosen for depositing the records here. …the filial principle of honoring one's parents, daily expressed in service at the Ciqing and Cining palaces. Setting forth the essentials in just a few hundred words, these teachings shine like the warp of Heaven and the weft of Earth; transmitting a standard for countless generations, they rise loftily beyond the achievements of emperors and kings. translation_en:
…for Your Majesty’s information.

Third Session: Five Policy Questions. First Question. Wang Feng.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor: For days, as I read the papers, I constantly feared overlooking a worthy candidate. When I came upon this candidate’s papers from the first two sessions, their talent and spirit were outstanding and untrammeled, powerful and profound—utterly distinctive. His five policy essays, moreover, answered the questions well. I have selected this essay because, beyond its expansive and exuberant praise, he is especially intent on personally expressing his loyalty. To have found such a worthy candidate gives us cause for congratulation.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor: The five answers display historical precedents, literary talent, and thoughtful ideas. In particular, he has thoroughly studied the excellence of our Emperor Zhang’s writings and is able to expound and extol them in his response. He must be a scholar of accumulated learning. This essay is selected as representative of the others.

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
廷對吾有望矣
天何為而立君也以出治也君何為而立
臣也以輔治也是故剛健中正運行而不
息者乾道也君也必體乎乾而後君道全
柔順利貞承天而時行者坤道也臣也必
體乎坤而後臣道舉君臣交盡其道而天
下之治成此我
宣宗章皇帝
帝訓官箴二書之所由作也大哉
===
皇言乎承天而立道體道而經世非天下之大
聖孰能與於此盖嘗嘉唐虞慕商周而有
以知其功用之盛矣請得而敬陳之今夫
唐虞之時何時也其君之相禪也則堯舜
禹天下之大聖也其臣之相師也則羲和
四嶽九官十二牧亦皆聖人之徒也夫以
聖而為君宜無待於告戒也然而執中慎
位之要每叮嚀於授受之間至其率作興
事以先諸臣也則又諄諄焉各舉其職以

translation_en:
…I have high hopes for your response at the Palace Examination.

Why does Heaven establish a ruler? To bring forth good government. Why does the ruler appoint ministers? To assist in governing. Thus, strength and vigor, centrality and rectitude, and ceaseless movement constitute the Way of Qian, Heaven. A ruler must embody Qian before the Way of the ruler can be complete. Gentleness and compliance, beneficial constancy, and following Heaven while acting in accord with the seasons constitute the Way of Kun, Earth. A minister must embody Kun before the Way of the minister can be fulfilled. When ruler and ministers each fully realize their Way, good government is achieved throughout the realm. This is why our Emperor Xuanzong Zhang composed the two books, Imperial Instructions and Admonitions for Officials. How great are these imperial words! To follow Heaven and establish the Way, to embody the Way and order the world—who but the greatest sage under Heaven could attain this? I have admired the ages of Tang and Yu and looked with longing upon Shang and Zhou, and have thereby come to understand the greatness of their achievements. Allow me respectfully to set this forth.

What sort of age was that of Tang and Yu? The rulers who successively yielded the throne were Yao, Shun, and Yu, the greatest sages under Heaven. Their ministers, who learned from one another—Xi and He, the Four Peaks, the Nine Officials, and the Twelve Governors—were likewise all followers of the sages. With sages as rulers, one might suppose that admonitions would be unnecessary. Yet the essentials of holding fast to the Mean and exercising care in occupying the throne were repeatedly urged whenever sovereignty was bestowed and received. When they led their ministers in undertaking work and initiating affairs, they again earnestly set forth each official’s duties in order to…

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
爲之訓是何其慮之遠而說之詳也哉誠
以爲君難爲臣不易儆戒相成之道不敢
以旣聖而輒懈也是以當時德業之盛高
明配天博厚配地而人至於今頌之不衰
有以哉三代相因其慮益遠而其爲訓也
益以詳其治功之成曰文命四敷曰兆民
允殖曰萬邦作孚卓乎上繼唐虞而非後
世所可得而及亦豈偶然哉自周以還此
意則微矣洪惟我
===
宣宗皇帝
睿資天縱
聖學日新念
太祖
太宗締造之惟艱思
後聖後賢守成之不易乃於萬幾之暇製爲
帝訓以示
神裔洋洋乎精一執中之格言其視禹有典則
之詒湯有風愆之儆文武有謨烈之啓佑

translation_en:
…to instruct them. How far-reaching his concerns, and how detailed his explanations! Truly, being a ruler is difficult, and being a minister is no easy matter. In mutually sustaining one another through admonition and warning, they dared not grow lax merely because they had already attained sagehood. Thus the flourishing virtue and achievements of that age matched Heaven in loftiness and brilliance and Earth in breadth and depth. There is good reason why people continue to praise them unabated even today! The Three Dynasties succeeded one another; their concerns reached ever further, and their instructions became ever more detailed. Of their achievements in government it was said: “His civilizing commands spread throughout the four quarters”; “The myriad people truly flourished”; and “The myriad states came to trust him.” Eminently continuing the accomplishments of Tang and Yu, they attained heights beyond the reach of later ages. Could this, too, have been mere chance? From the Zhou onward, this spirit faded.
We reverently reflect that our Xuanzong Emperor, endowed by Heaven with sagacious gifts and daily advancing in the learning of the sages, considered the hardships Taizu and Taizong had endured in founding the dynasty, and pondered the difficulty that later sage and worthy rulers would face in preserving their inheritance. Thus, in the intervals between his myriad affairs of state, he composed Imperial Instructions (Dixun) to instruct his august descendants. How abundant its exemplary sayings on refinement and single-mindedness, and on holding fast to the mean! Compared with Yu’s bequest of statutes and standards, Tang’s warnings against wayward habits and faults, and the guidance and assistance provided by the plans and achievements of Kings Wen and Wu…

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
不啻匹休而已是誠萬世爲君者之蓍蔡
也又製爲官箴以示百工鑿鑿乎吁咈疇
咨之至訓其視夏有定保之謨商有官刑
之制周有周官之誥飭又不啻媲美而已
是誠萬世爲臣者之準繩也自今觀之
帝訓之爲目凡二十有五首之以君德所以脩
身也終之以藥餌養身所以養德也諸如
奉天法祖之訓正家睦親之訓仁民經國
勤政之訓恭儉儆戒之訓用賢知人之訓
===
去邪防微之訓重農興學之訓祭祀恤刑
之訓賞罰黜陟之訓文治武備之訓馭夷
之訓盖不一而足也是其爲書統會乎天
人參稽乎今古以俟來聖則不惑以考前
聖則有徵夫豈漢文之法術唐太宗之帝
範眞宗之承華要畧或舉用而遺體或崇
利而薄義者可得而擬哉官箴之爲目凡
三十有五首之以督府所以經武也終之
以儒學修文所以偃武也諸如六部都察

…it does far more than merely equal their excellence. It is truly an oracle of milfoil stalks and tortoise shells for rulers of all ages. He also composed Admonitions for Officials (Guanzhen) to instruct the entire officialdom. How authoritative are these supreme instructions in consultation and candid counsel! Compared with the Xia dynasty’s counsels for securing lasting stability, the Shang dynasty’s regulations on punishments for officials, and the Zhou dynasty’s proclamations and injunctions in “The Officials of Zhou,” it likewise does far more than merely match their excellence. It is truly a measuring line for ministers of all ages.
Examining the Imperial Instructions (Dixun) now, we find twenty-five headings in all. It begins with the ruler’s virtue, as the means of cultivating oneself; it ends with medicines and nourishment for the body, as the means of nurturing virtue. Its instructions include serving Heaven and emulating the ancestors; setting the household in order and maintaining harmony among relatives; showing benevolence to the people, ordering the state, and attending diligently to government; reverence, frugality, and vigilance; employing the worthy and discerning people’s character; removing evil and guarding against its slightest beginnings; giving weight to agriculture and promoting learning; sacrifices and compassion in administering punishment; rewards and punishments, dismissals and promotions; civil governance and military preparedness; and managing the non-Chinese peoples. These are too numerous to enumerate fully. As a book, it brings together Heaven and humanity and examines past and present against one another. One may await future sages without misgivings about it, and test it against former sages and find corroboration. How could the governing methods of Emperor Wen of Han, the Model for Emperors (Difan) of Taizong of Tang, or the Essential Outline for the Heir Apparent (Chenghua yaolüe) of Zhenzong—which either emphasize practical application while neglecting underlying principles, or exalt advantage while slighting righteousness—possibly be compared with it?
Admonitions for Officials has thirty-five headings in all. It begins with the chief military commissions, as the means of ordering military affairs; it ends with the Confucian schools and the cultivation of civil learning, as the means of laying arms to rest. Among its subjects are the Six Ministries and the Censorate…

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
院之箴太常大理通政之箴詹事翰林之
箴春坊經局之箴光祿鴻臚太僕之箴國
學欽天京府之箴六科行人之箴錦衣留
守之箴都司諸衛之箴藩臬守令之箴王
官鹺使之箴蓋秩然具談也是其爲書合
内外而揆叙舉文武而并苞以令則爲象
魏之布法以教則爲皇極之敷言夫豈漢
續虞人之箴唐試理人之策宋賜訓廉謹
刑之銘或假手於臣下或蹈迹於古人者
===
可得而班哉夫二書之綱領者蓋如此而
聖意之淵微則又於二序見之則愚於前既發
其端矣請遂得而究言之可乎彼訓之序
有曰天心仁愛下民爰命君以主之故君
行必如天之健斯言也即乾之日乾夕惕
之義也夫人君而苟以體乾爲心則必憂
勤兢業一念不謹恐貽四海之憂一時不
謹恐致千百年之患是故朝以聽政也必
公卿訓告諫諍陳列而無敢怠於朝晝以

院之箴，太常、大理、通政之箴，詹事、翰林之箴，春坊、經局之箴，光祿、鴻臚、太僕之箴，國學、欽天、京府之箴，六科、行人之箴，錦衣、留守之箴，都司、諸衛之箴，藩臬、守令之箴，王官、鹺使之箴，蓋秩然具談也。是其爲書，合内外而揆叙，舉文武而并苞，以令則爲象魏之布法，以教則爲皇極之敷言。夫豈漢續《虞人》之箴，唐試理人之策，宋賜訓廉謹刑之銘，或假手於臣下，或蹈迹於古人者，可得而班哉？
夫二書之綱領者，蓋如此。而聖意之淵微，則又於二序見之。則愚於前既發其端矣，請遂得而究言之，可乎？彼訓之序有曰：「天心仁愛下民，爰命君以主之，故君行必如天之健。」斯言也，即《乾》之日乾夕惕之義也。夫人君而苟以體乾爲心，則必憂勤兢業，一念不謹，恐貽四海之憂；一時不謹，恐致千百年之患。是故朝以聽政也，必公卿訓告，諫諍陳列，而無敢怠於朝；晝以

…admonitions for the Censorate; those for the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Court of Judicial Review, and Office of Transmission; those for the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent and Hanlin Academy; those for the Spring Offices and the Classics Office; those for the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Court of State Ceremonial, and Court of the Imperial Stud; those for the National University, Directorate of Astronomy, and metropolitan prefectures; those for the Six Offices of Scrutiny and the messengers; those for the Embroidered-uniform Guard and the regency offices; those for the Regional Military Commissions and the various guards; those for the provincial administration and surveillance commissions, prefects, and magistrates; and those for princely officials and salt commissioners—all are discussed fully and in orderly fashion. This book embraces both central and local government, arranging their responsibilities, and encompasses civil and military affairs alike. As commands, its words are laws promulgated at the palace gate towers; as instruction, they are an exposition of the August Norm. How could it be ranked alongside the Han continuation of the Admonition of the Forester, the Tang policy questions on governing the people, or the Song inscriptions bestowed to inculcate integrity and caution in punishment—works either entrusted to subjects or following in the footsteps of the ancients?
Such, broadly, are the guiding principles of these two books. The profound subtleties of the imperial intent are further revealed in their two prefaces. Having already introduced the subject above, may I now pursue it in full? The preface to those Instructions says: “Heaven’s heart benevolently loves the people below, and therefore appoints a ruler to preside over them. Thus the ruler’s conduct must resemble Heaven’s vigor.” These words express precisely the meaning of the Qian hexagram’s injunction to be vigorous throughout the day and vigilant in the evening. If a ruler truly sets his heart on embodying Qian, he will assuredly be solicitous, diligent, cautious, and conscientious. title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
訪問也必揚確古今周諏民物而無敢怠
於晝夕以修令也必慎而後出奠而後發
而無敢怠於夕推是心也以往則於前之
所謂二十有五事者將恐恐然體之弗遑
矣而暇逸乎是則訓之精意也於我
文皇聖學心法所謂君道之旨盖闡明而無遺
矣箴之序有曰隆古盛時君臣交儆而卒
期於謀猷之樂聞斯言也即坤之含章從
王之義也夫人臣苟以從王為心則必鞠
===
恭盡瘁一曰立乎其位則一曰業乎其官
一日不得乎其官則不敢一日立乎其位
是故大而服休也為阿衡之任為赤舃之

When revising ordinances in the evening, he must exercise care before issuing them and settle them firmly before promulgating them, never daring to be remiss in the evening. If a minister truly sets his heart on following the king, he will surely bow in reverence and expend all his strength. For each day that he occupies his position, he must attend to the duties of his office; if for even one day he cannot properly discharge those duties, he must not dare remain in his position for that day. Thus, at the highest level, those entrusted with honored service shoulder the responsibilities of an Aheng, or chief minister, and show the reverence befitting the wearer of red ceremonial shoes, yet dare not regard this as sufficient loyalty. At the next level, those charged with administrative duties maintain the selfless integrity of one who disregards his own person and the dutifulness of one who remedies disorder, yet dare not regard this as an achievement. title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
聖祖資世通訓所謂臣用之旨盖對揚而無斁
矣嗚呼訓昭于上而出治者有所持循箴
行于下而輔治者由之警動是以百餘年
來上而
勳華纘序下而謨弼奏功盖已燦然畢覩其効
矣今
聖天子在上又從而振揚光大之
昭德建中本之以敬一之學明法飭令申之
以久大之規上下交而泰道新明良會而
===
賡歌作盖不出善繼善述之孝而有以溥
會極歸極之化矣詩不云乎世德作求永
言配命成王之孚下土之式愚請誦此以
獻

陳濡

士類能敷演成文至酌古準今確有定論如此
作者絕少且他作才氣浩博亦復稱是獨對

聖祖《資世通訓》所謂臣用之旨，盖對揚而無斁矣。嗚呼！訓昭于上，而出治者有所持循；箴行于下，而輔治者由之警動。是以百餘年來，上而勳華纘序，下而謨弼奏功，盖已燦然畢覩其効矣。今聖天子在上，又從而振揚光大之。昭德建中，本之以敬一之學；明法飭令，申之以久大之規。上下交而泰道新，明良會而賡歌作，盖不出善繼善述之孝，而有以溥會極歸極之化矣。《詩》不云乎：「世德作求，永言配命。成王之孚，下土之式。」愚請誦此以獻。

第二問

陳濡

同考試官學正錢批：祀戎一策，塲中諸士類能敷演成文，至酌古準今，確有定論如此作者絕少。且他作才氣浩博，亦復稱是。獨對
translation_en:
…the principle concerning the employment of ministers set forth in our Sagely Ancestor’s Comprehensive Instructions for Aiding the World (Zishi tongxun) has thus been acknowledged and exalted without weariness. Ah! The instructions shine forth above, giving those who govern something to uphold and follow; the admonitions circulate below, stirring those who assist in government to vigilance. Thus, for more than a hundred years, rulers above have continued the succession of Yao and Shun, while ministers below have achieved results through counsel and assistance. The effects have already been splendidly manifest in full.

Now the Sagely Son of Heaven reigns above and further promotes and magnifies these teachings. In manifesting virtue and establishing the mean, he takes as his foundation the learning of reverent unity; in clarifying laws and putting commands in order, he reinforces them with plans of enduring and far-reaching scope. Those above and below communicate, renewing the way of harmonious prosperity; an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers meet, and responsive songs arise. All this proceeds from the filial devotion that worthily continues and carries forward the work of one’s predecessors, thereby extending the transforming influence through which all assemble at and turn toward the supreme standard. Does not the Book of Odes say: “Seek to continue the virtue of successive generations; ever strive to accord with Heaven’s mandate. King Cheng’s trustworthiness is the model for the lands below”? I humbly ask leave to recite these words as my offering.

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
大廷盖于子有望矣
考試官洗馬歐陽批處置曲當議論英發
豈嘗慮及
廟堂者耶他日事業于此乎占矣
考試官左諭德江批此問關涉理道最大
非有志經世者則漫不知省矣子能商確古今
以求是當將不謂俊傑士耶
帝王之理天下也有報本之大禮有經武
之大政盖禮莫重於祀也而郊禋廟饗所
===
以報本尤為禮之大政莫重於戎也而選
將治兵所以經武尤為政之大政成而保
大定功天下無不威禮行而體信達順天
下無不化此古先帝王致理之大經而我
皇上之所獨造而優為之者也盖常聞諸奉常
質諸本兵而有以得其槩矣請敬述以對
今夫
二郊分祀古禮也自夫同牢之儀黷於漢而此
禮湮盖二千餘年于兹矣惟我

帝王之理天下也，有報本之大禮，有經武之大政。盖禮莫重於祀也，而郊禋廟饗所以報本，尤為禮之大；政莫重於戎也，而選將治兵所以經武，尤為政之大。政成而保大定功，天下無不威；禮行而體信達順，天下無不化。此古先帝王致理之大經，而我皇上之所獨造而優為之者也。盖常聞諸奉常，質諸本兵，而有以得其槩矣。請敬述以對。

…before the imperial court: surely there is much to hope for from you.
Examiner Ouyang, Librarian, comments: Your proposed measures are fitting in every particular, and your arguments are brilliant. Have you perhaps already given thought to affairs of the imperial government? Your future achievements may be foretold from this.
Examiner Jiang, Left Mentor, comments: This question bears most substantially upon the principles of government. Anyone without a commitment to ordering the world would heedlessly fail to reflect upon it. You have critically weighed past and present to seek what is right and fitting. How could you not be called an outstanding scholar?
When emperors and kings govern the world, they have great rites for requiting the sources of their existence and great policies for managing military affairs. Among rites, none is weightier than sacrifice; the suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth and the offerings in the ancestral temples, through which those sources are requited, are especially momentous rites. Among affairs of government, none is weightier than warfare; selecting generals and training troops, through which military affairs are managed, are especially momentous policies. When these policies succeed, preserving greatness and securing achievements, none under Heaven fails to stand in awe. When these rites are performed, embodying trustworthiness and bringing about concord, none under Heaven fails to be transformed. These are the great guiding principles by which the emperors and kings of antiquity brought about good government, and in these our Emperor has attained unique heights and acted with surpassing excellence. I have heard of them from the officials responsible for sacrifices and verified them with those responsible for military affairs, and have thereby gained an understanding of their broad outlines. I respectfully beg leave to recount them in reply.

punctuated: 皇上聰明聖知，上達天德，卓然起而修復之，而精義妙用則又發之於聖諭。有曰：「南北二郊俱以高皇帝奉配。」言有尊也。有曰：「歲首仍祀上帝於大祀殿，以文皇帝奉配。」言有親也。大哉，皇言乎！唯仁饗帝，唯孝饗親，真一言而世爲天下則矣乎！然而歲首奉配之儀，兹若小異於聖諭者，其諸將事之臣庸有執其咎者乎？嘗聞諸經：「周人郊祀后稷以配天，宗祀文王於明堂以配上帝。」而先儒陳氏亦曰：「郊而曰天，所以尊之也；配以后稷，亦以尊后稷也。明堂而曰帝，所以親之也；配以文王，亦以親文王也。尊尊而親親，周道備矣。」此聖諭之精所以妙契周公之心也。且禮有之：「有其舉之，莫敢廢也。」所謂大祀殿者，巋然于南郊，則與《大戴禮》《韓詩傳》諸
translation_en:
…Your Majesty, endowed with keen perception and sagely wisdom, comprehending above the virtue of Heaven, resolutely arose to restore these rites. Their profound principles and subtle application were further elucidated in your sagely instructions. One passage states: “At both the southern and northern suburban altars, Emperor Gao shall be associated with the principal recipient of sacrifice.” This expresses reverence. Another states: “At the beginning of the year, continue to sacrifice to the Lord on High in the Hall of the Great Sacrifice, with Emperor Wen associated with him.” This expresses familial affection. How great are these imperial words! Only through benevolence can one offer acceptable sacrifice to the Lord on High; only through filial devotion can one offer acceptable sacrifice to one's parents. Truly, is this not a single pronouncement that will serve as a standard for all under Heaven for generations? Yet the rite of associating an ancestor with the principal recipient at the beginning of the year now seems to differ slightly from your sagely instructions. Might some of the officials conducting the ceremony bear responsibility for this?

I have heard it stated in the classics: “The people of Zhou sacrificed to Hou Ji at the suburban altar, associating him with Heaven; they offered ancestral sacrifice to King Wen in the Hall of Light, associating him with the Lord on High.” The earlier Confucian scholar Chen also said: “At the suburban altar, the designation ‘Heaven’ expresses reverence; associating Hou Ji with Heaven likewise expresses reverence for Hou Ji. In the Hall of Light, the designation ‘Lord’ expresses familial affection; associating King Wen with him likewise expresses familial affection for King Wen. By revering those worthy of reverence and cherishing one's kin, the Way of Zhou is complete.” Thus the refined meaning of your sagely instructions accords wondrously with the mind of the Duke of Zhou.

Moreover, the ritual text says: “When these rites are performed [?], none dares abolish them.” The so-called Hall of the Great Sacrifice stands imposingly in the southern suburbs; it thus accords with the various … in the Elder Dai's Record of Rites (Da Dai Li) and Han's Commentary on the Odes (Han Shi Zhuan) …

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄

辨固在所畧者也誠如
聖諭則不煩更制之勞而周道燦然復興矣是
豈惟處禮之精而制義之妙不亦行于其
間乎
九廟異制亦古禮也自夫同堂之儀殽於漢而
此制湮盖亦二千餘年于茲矣惟我

德祖而合以

天下法矣乎然而

punctuated:
說靡有不同，而呂氏《考功記》區區制度之辨，固在所畧者也。誠如聖諭，則不煩更制之勞，而周道燦然復興矣。是豈惟處禮之精，而制義之妙不亦行于其間乎？

九廟異制，亦古禮也。自夫同堂之儀殽於漢，而此制湮，盖亦二千餘年于茲矣。惟我皇上仁孝誠敬，洞契古始，慨然起而修復之，而鴻彜曠軌，則又斷之於神衷。肇舉大禘之典，尊祀皇初祖，而配以太祖；裁定大祫之圖，尊祀德祖，而合以列祖。至哉，皇猷乎！以作則謂聖，以述則謂明，真行而世為天下法矣乎！然而
translation_en:
…these accounts all agree, while the petty distinctions concerning institutional arrangements in Master Lü’s Record of Examining Achievements (Kaogong ji) [?] are surely matters that may be passed over. If the imperial instruction is indeed followed, there will be no need for the toil of changing the institutions, and the Way of Zhou will rise again in splendor. Is this merely refinement in the handling of ritual? Does not the subtle skill of establishing what is right also operate within it?

The arrangement of nine separate ancestral temples is likewise an ancient rite. Since the practice of housing the ancestors in a single hall confused the rites in the Han dynasty, this arrangement has fallen into obscurity—for more than two thousand years now. Our Emperor alone, through his benevolence, filial devotion, sincerity, and reverence, has profoundly apprehended the ancient beginnings and resolutely undertaken their restoration. These grand enduring norms and long-neglected precedents have moreover been settled in his sagely heart. He first instituted the great di sacrifice, reverently sacrificing to the imperial First Progenitor and associating Taizu with him; he determined the plan for the great xia joint sacrifice, reverently sacrificing to Dezu and bringing the successive ancestors together with him. How perfect is the imperial design! To institute is called sageliness; to transmit is called discernment. Truly, his conduct will serve for generations as a model for all under Heaven! Yet…

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
諸王祔食勳臣從享之節尚若有待于
聖裁者其諸節目之微固亦在所畧矣乎嘗聞
諸禮殤與無後者從祖祔食而伊川亦曰
祭終兄弟之孫之身蓋從祖而祔則亦從
祖而毁也惡有正享之祖已祧而
諸王之以班祔食者乃顧獨存耶此其存罷
之節有可得而裁者矣周禮司勳凡有功
者書于太常祭於大烝而書盤庚亦曰兹
予大享於先王爾祖其從與享之言祫烝
===
也其禴祀嘗則固弗與也惡有世室之主
歲凡五祀而諸臣之以功從享者顧等而
上之耶此其疏數之節有可得而裁者矣
於戲禮行於廟而孝慈服禮行於郊而百
神受職焉帝王化成之道孰有大於此是
惡得而弗慎矣乎以選將言之古者因六
鄉而置帥其擇吏也固所以擇將也自夫
世禄任而文武分於是有紈袴之將矣儲
材待用其惟武舉乎然而試之以騎射末

translation_en:
…As for the rules governing the princes’ participation in ancestral offerings and meritorious ministers’ attendance at sacrifices, these still seem to await Your Majesty’s sagely decision. Can such finer points of ritual procedure really be left aside? I have heard it stated in the ritual texts that those who die prematurely or leave no descendants receive subsidiary offerings with their ancestors. Yichuan also said: “Their sacrifices end with the lifetimes of their brothers’ grandsons.” Since they are associated with an ancestor in receiving offerings, their worship must also cease when that ancestor’s shrine is dismantled. How could an ancestor who receives the principal offerings already have been removed from his shrine, while the princes who receive subsidiary offerings according to their generational rank alone remain? Here, then, is a matter of retention or discontinuance that can be settled by imperial decision.

In the Rites of Zhou, the Director of Merits records all who have rendered meritorious service on the grand banner, and they receive sacrifices at the great winter sacrifice. The “Pan Geng” chapter of the Book of Documents likewise says: “When I make a great offering to the former kings, your ancestors will accompany them and share in the offering.” This refers to the combined ancestral sacrifice in winter. They certainly do not participate in the yue, si, and chang seasonal sacrifices. How could the spirit tablets in the permanent ancestral chambers receive five sacrifices each year, while the ministers who attend the sacrifices by virtue of their merits are actually placed above them in frequency of worship? Here, then, is a matter of more or less frequent observance that can be settled by imperial decision.

Ah! When rites are performed in the ancestral temple, filial devotion and parental affection are put into practice; when rites are performed at the suburban altar, the hundred spirits receive their appointed duties. Among the means by which emperors and kings perfect their transforming influence, what could be greater than this? How, then, could one fail to exercise care?

Speaking of the selection of generals: in antiquity, commanders were appointed on the basis of the six townships. Selecting civil officers was thus also the means of selecting generals. Once emoluments and appointments became hereditary and civil and military functions were separated, generals drawn from privileged young dandies appeared. For building a reserve of talent awaiting employment, should we not look to the military examinations? Yet to examine candidates in mounted archery is to test a minor…

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
技也固有絶藝如陵而終則爲虜者試之
以策論空文也固有知書如括而用之輒
敗者安得不厪
當宁拊髀之歎哉頃者
皇上講武之議盖誠有意於是矣愚則曰蓄材
靡豫也制用靡慎也舊敝未芟而新敝吾
恐其復滋也何也
祖宗之於武臣也勲裔則養之國學世胄則肄
之衛學其在天下則又育之於各學所以
===
需其材而用之者未嘗不至也顧漢法酎
金逮於徹侯今則貂蟬孰罰矣何以破其
苟且之心城旦附於介胄今則節鉞安土
矣何以作其激昻之氣自非一大振厲之
則亦何以成其材而舉之哉是故丹書之
信誠不可渝矣而保祿之誥則宜從而飭
之矢石之勞誠不可負矣而比試之條則
宜從而覈之盖必有以怵其舊而後韜畧
可課也治兵可嘗也蓄之既豫而羅之庶

之矢石之勞誠不可負矣而比試之條則
宜從而覈之盖必有以怵其舊而後韜畧

punctuated:
技也。固有絶藝如陵，而終則爲虜者；試之以策論，空文也。固有知書如括，而用之輒敗者。安得不厪當宁拊髀之歎哉？頃者，皇上講武之議，盖誠有意於是矣。愚則曰：蓄材靡豫也，制用靡慎也。舊敝未芟，而新敝吾恐其復滋也。何也？祖宗之於武臣也，勲裔則養之國學，世胄則肄之衛學，其在天下則又育之於各學，所以需其材而用之者，未嘗不至也。
顧漢法酎金逮於徹侯，今則貂蟬孰罰矣？何以破其苟且之心？城旦附於介胄，今則節鉞安土矣，何以作其激昻之氣？自非一大振厲之，則亦何以成其材而舉之哉？是故丹書之信，誠不可渝矣，而保祿之誥，則宜從而飭之；矢石之勞，誠不可負矣，而比試之條，則宜從而覈之。盖必有以怵其舊，而後韜畧可課也，治兵可嘗也。蓄之既豫，而羅之庶
translation_en:
…minor skills. There have certainly been men with exceptional prowess like Li Ling who nevertheless ended up as captives. To test them through policy essays and discourses is to test empty writing. There have certainly been men versed in books like Zhao Kuo who invariably met defeat when employed. How could this fail to trouble the sovereign, making him slap his thigh and sigh for a worthy general? His Majesty’s recent proposal to conduct military exercises surely reflects a genuine concern with this matter. In my humble view, talent is not being cultivated in advance, nor is its employment managed with due care. Before the old abuses have been eliminated, I fear that new ones will proliferate. Why is this? In their treatment of military officers, our imperial ancestors educated the descendants of meritorious men in the National University, trained the sons of hereditary military families in the guard schools, and further educated those throughout the realm in the various local schools. Their arrangements for awaiting the maturation of these men’s talents and employing them were never less than thorough.
Yet under Han law, penalties concerning gold offerings for the ancestral sacrifices extended even to marquises. Today, who among those wearing the sable-and-cicada insignia of high office is punished? How can their disposition to muddle along be broken? Even convicts sentenced to wall-building served among the armored troops; today, those bearing the tally and battle-axe of command remain comfortably settled in their own localities. How can their fighting spirit be roused? Without a great effort to stir and discipline them, how can their talents be developed and they themselves advanced? Thus, the pledges recorded in the vermilion documents of investiture must indeed remain inviolate, but the patents guaranteeing their emoluments should accordingly be reinforced with admonitions. Their labors amid arrows and stones must indeed not go unrewarded, but the regulations governing comparative military tests should accordingly be rigorously enforced. There must be some means of shaking them out of their old habits before their strategic abilities can be assessed and their skill in managing troops put to the test. Once talent has been cultivated in advance and efforts made to gather it, perhaps…

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
乎可得也何謂制用盖將材既得矣任之
弗專不可也則操斧以授而間色無可窺
流言無可動也任之既專矣待之弗厚不
可也則豐犒以資而養士為之資內顧為
之恤也不幸而罹眚也則姑畧之雖謗書
盈篋而不惑何也小廉細謹非所以繩武
弁也又不幸而失律也則必懲之雖揮淚
臨刑而不恤何也信賞決罰所以振吾之
紀綱也如是則制用惟慎而御將之道斯
===
得矣以治兵言之古者因井田而制兵其
容民也固所以蓄眾也自夫井田廢而兵
農分於是有坐食之兵矣寓兵於農其惟
府兵乎今之兵既不可轉而之農矣而農
之廪於兵者日益增今之農既困於兵矣
而兵之力日益以不足是惡得而不遺
九重宵旰之慮哉往者
皇上募兵之令盖亦有意於是矣愚則曰冗兵
弗汰也虛兵弗祛也吾恐兵益增而民益

乎可得也。何謂制用？盖將材既得矣，任之弗專不可也，則操斧以授，而間色無可窺，流言無可動也。任之既專矣，待之弗厚不可也，則豐犒以資，而養士為之資，內顧為之恤也。不幸而罹眚也，則姑畧之，雖謗書盈篋而不惑。何也？小廉細謹，非所以繩武弁也。又不幸而失律也，則必懲之，雖揮淚臨刑而不恤。何也？信賞決罰，所以振吾之紀綱也。如是，則制用惟慎，而御將之道斯得矣。
以治兵言之，古者因井田而制兵，其容民也，固所以蓄眾也。自夫井田廢而兵農分，於是有坐食之兵矣。寓兵於農，其惟府兵乎？今之兵既不可轉而之農矣，而農之廪於兵者日益增；今之農既困於兵矣，而兵之力日益以不足。是惡得而不遺九重宵旰之慮哉？往者皇上募兵之令，盖亦有意於是矣。愚則曰：冗兵弗汰也，虛兵弗祛也，吾恐兵益增而民益
translation_en:
…they may perhaps be secured. What is meant by controlling and employing commanders? Once talented commanders have been found, they must be given undivided authority. Accordingly, confer the battle-axe upon them, leaving no opening for signs of wavering confidence [?] and allowing no rumors to shake that confidence. Once they have been entrusted with undivided authority, they must be treated generously. Supply them with ample rewards, provide the means to maintain their men, and relieve their worries about their families. If they should unfortunately incur some fault, overlook it for the time being; even if slanderous letters fill a chest, do not be misled. Why? Scrupulousness in petty matters and meticulous caution are not the standards by which military officers should be judged. If, however, they should suffer a failure of military discipline, they must be punished; even if one sheds tears at the execution, one must not spare them. Why? Reliable rewards and resolute punishments uphold our governing order. In this way, with due care in controlling and employing them, the proper way to govern commanders will be attained.
As for administering the troops, the ancients organized their armies on the basis of the well-field system. Their provision for the people was precisely the means of maintaining a body of fighting men. Once the well-field system was abolished and soldiers and farmers became separate, soldiers emerged who consumed provisions without producing them. Was it not the garrison militia system (fubing) that embedded soldiers among the farming population? Today’s soldiers cannot be converted into farmers, yet the provisions farmers supply to soldiers increase daily. Today’s farmers are already impoverished by the burden of supporting soldiers, yet military strength grows ever less adequate. How could this fail to cause His Majesty, deep within the palace, anxiety that keeps him up before dawn and delays his evening meal? His Majesty’s earlier order to recruit soldiers surely also addressed this concern. In my humble view, however, if superfluous soldiers are not discharged and fictitious soldiers are not removed from the rolls, I fear that the troops will increase while the people become ever more…

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
以困也何也
祖宗之於兵政也七十二衛嘗敝矣則救之以
三大營三大營又敝矣則又救之以十二
團營所以閱其實而練之者未嘗不備也
顧法以久玩而羸病之卒率糜廩於轅門
政以賄成而影射之徒又納貲於奸橐自
非一大簡稽之則亦何以剔其蠹而養之
哉必也責之臺諫行視於教閱之地則老
壯勇怯既可以槩見責之本兵檢括於司
===
籍之人則死生存亡又可以周知由是而
太祖弛備之律可行也由是而
太宗失伍之令可行也而冗兵庶乎可汰矣若
夫所謂虛兵者則有其名而無其人也無
其人而有其食也夫無人而有食則其食
也誰食之是必有私之者矣彼執籍以責
吾之食也而吾亦按籍而餽之食是私之
者誠利也而民則不勝其病矣於是乎悉
覈之而以其食廩乎代補之新兵則投石

若夫所謂虛兵者，則有其名而無其人也，無其人而有其食也。夫無人而有食，則其食也誰食之？是必有私之者矣。彼執籍以責吾之食也，而吾亦按籍而餽之食，是私之者誠利也，而民則不勝其病矣。於是乎悉覈之，而以其食廩乎代補之新兵，則投石
translation_en:
…thereby become more impoverished. Why is this? In our imperial ancestors’ administration of military affairs, when the seventy-two Guards had fallen into decay, they remedied this by establishing the Three Great Training Divisions. When these in turn declined, they again remedied matters by establishing the Twelve Regimental Camps. Their provisions for inspecting actual troop strength and training the men were never less than comprehensive. Yet as the regulations became familiar through long use, they were treated lightly, and weak and sickly soldiers generally squandered provisions within the camps. Official business was settled through bribery, and men fraudulently claiming military status paid money into corrupt officials’ purses. Without a thorough muster and audit, how could these abuses be rooted out and the troops properly supported? The censors and remonstrance officials must be charged with personally inspecting the training grounds: then the old and the vigorous, the brave and the timid, can be assessed in broad outline. The Minister of War must be charged with checking the records held by those responsible for the registers: then who is dead or alive, present or absent, can be fully ascertained. Through this, Taizu’s statute against neglecting military preparedness can be enforced; through this, Taizong’s order against leaving the ranks can be enforced. Thus there may be hope of eliminating superfluous soldiers.

篇

大廷之對尚有望於子矣
善言天者徵諸民而已矣善事天者恤夫
民而已矣盖天人一道君民一體論天而
不徵諸民則索之於冥漠其究也誕應天
而不恤夫民則索之於儀文其究也偽是
尚足與語天人相與之際也哉是故異眾
而戒未必不安戒之云何憂其民也民安
而國亦安矣祥多而恃未必不危恃之云
何忽其民也民危而國亦危矣皐陶以天

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之聰明明威達于上下召公以誠小民爲
祈天永命之本道有二乎哉愚也嘗讀甘
石巫咸之書正之以洪範春秋之傳而又
旁觀乎漢儒陰陽之說於其所不知盖闕
如矣請即其所明者以復明問可乎夫一
陰一陽之謂道天地間盡之矣試觀之陽
一舒焉則天地萬物不約而皆喜陰一慘
焉則天地萬物不約而皆戚夫物則亦有
然者矣而况人與天地本同一體其精神
===
有以相盪其志氣有以相召者乎夫眾人
則亦有然者矣而况大君天地之宗子大
臣宗子之家相其威命靈爽與造化相出
入者乎盖嘗觀董仲舒曰人君所爲美惡
之極與天地流通而往來相應是若不及
於民矣然所爲之美惡即民心之向背未
有天地位而萬物不育者又嘗觀吕祖謙
曰治天下者不盡人之財不盡人之力不
盡人之情是若不及於天矣然民心之好

…Heaven’s keenness of hearing and sight and its manifest awe communicate between those above and below; the Duke of Shao regarded sincerity toward the common people as the foundation for praying to Heaven for an enduring mandate. Could there be two Ways? I, in my ignorance, have read the writings of Gan, Shi, and Wu Xian, checked them against the commentaries on the Great Plan and the Spring and Autumn Annals, and also surveyed the Han scholars’ explanations of yin and yang. Where I lack understanding, I have left the matter unresolved. May I answer your discerning question on the basis of what I do understand?

The alternation of yin and yang is called the Way: this encompasses everything between Heaven and Earth. Consider: when yang unfolds, all things in Heaven and Earth rejoice without concerted agreement; when yin grows bleak, all things in Heaven and Earth grieve without concerted agreement. If this is true even of things, how much more must it be true of human beings, who originally form one body with Heaven and Earth, whose vital spirits can stir one another and whose intentions and vital energies can call forth responses from one another? If this is true even of ordinary people, how much more must it be true of the sovereign, the principal heir of Heaven and Earth, and the great ministers, the stewards of that heir’s household, whose commanding authority and numinous intelligence participate in the workings of creation?

I have read Dong Zhongshu’s statement: “The utmost good and evil in a ruler’s conduct flow through Heaven and Earth, passing back and forth in mutual response.” This seems not to concern the people. Yet the good and evil of his conduct are precisely what determine whether the people’s hearts turn toward him or away from him. Never have Heaven and Earth occupied their proper places without the myriad things flourishing. I have also read Lü Zuqian’s statement: “Those who govern all under Heaven do not exhaust the people’s wealth, do not exhaust the people’s strength, and do not press their feelings to the limit.” This seems not to concern Heaven. title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
惡即天心之從違未有民心悅而天意不
得者二子之見其有異乎哉故漢文之時
以長星則出天也以大水則潰地也以日
食旱蝗則常常而見也然恭修玄默力行
恭儉露臺惜百金之費後宮無曳地之衣
可謂不盡人之財者矣匈奴三出於塞外
霸陵一因其山制可謂不盡人之力者矣
吳王不朝賜以几杖張武受賂遺以金錢
惴惴然恐人情之或盡也使能納禮樂之
===
疏其治之所就豈可量乎漢武之時以天
馬則升歌也以狩獸則紀元也以寶鼎芝
房則紛紛而是也然雄才大畧好大喜功
錢幣取極於錙銖糜費用同於泥沙財盡
有不勝其求者矣票騎雲擾於狼胥烏孫
日通於酒泉力疲有不勝其役者矣湯禹
之刻深連根抵淮衡之慘究極黨與汲汲
然恐民情之不盡也是雖有輪臺之悔其
國之所存亦云幸耳由是言之有災之文

惡，即天心之從違，未有民心悅而天意不得者。二子之見，其有異乎哉？故漢文之時，以長星則出天也，以大水則潰地也，以日食旱蝗則常常而見也。然恭修玄默，力行恭儉，露臺惜百金之費，後宮無曳地之衣，可謂不盡人之財者矣。匈奴三出於塞外，霸陵一因其山制，可謂不盡人之力者矣。吳王不朝，賜以几杖；張武受賂，遺以金錢：惴惴然恐人情之或盡也。使能納禮樂之疏，其治之所就豈可量乎？

漢武之時，以天馬則升歌也，以狩獸則紀元也，以寶鼎芝房則紛紛而是也。然雄才大畧，好大喜功，錢幣取極於錙銖，糜費用同於泥沙，財盡有不勝其求者矣。票騎雲擾於狼胥，烏孫日通於酒泉，力疲有不勝其役者矣。湯禹之刻深，連根抵；淮衡之慘，究極黨與：汲汲然恐民情之不盡也。是雖有輪臺之悔，其國之所存亦云幸耳。由是言之，有災之文
translation_en:
…and dislikes are precisely what determines Heaven’s approval or disapproval. Never have the people’s hearts been pleased without Heaven’s will being fulfilled. Could the views of these two thinkers really differ? Thus, in the time of Emperor Wen of Han, comets appeared in the heavens, great floods devastated the land, and solar eclipses, droughts, and locust plagues occurred repeatedly. Yet he reverently cultivated quietude and earnestly practiced humility and frugality. He begrudged the expenditure of a hundred jin of gold on the Dew Terrace, and the women of his palace wore no robes that trailed along the ground. He may indeed be said not to have exhausted the people’s wealth. The Xiongnu were driven beyond the frontier three times [?], and his tomb at Baling was fashioned entirely according to the mountain’s natural form. He may indeed be said not to have exhausted the people’s strength. When the Prince of Wu failed to attend court, he bestowed an armrest and a staff upon him; when Zhang Wu accepted bribes, he presented him with money. He was anxiously concerned lest the people’s goodwill be exhausted. Had he been able to accept the memorial concerning rites and music, how could the achievements of his government have been measured?

In the time of Emperor Wu of Han, the heavenly horse was celebrated in ceremonial song, the capture of a beast gave a reign period its name, and auspicious treasures such as precious tripods and numinous fungi appeared in profusion. Yet, for all his extraordinary abilities and grand strategies, he delighted in great undertakings and coveted achievements. He exacted money down to the smallest fraction and squandered it like mud and sand. With their wealth exhausted, some could no longer meet his demands. The General of Swift Cavalry stirred like clouds about Langxu, while communications with Wusun passed daily through Jiuquan. With their strength depleted, some could no longer bear his demands for service. The harshness of Tang and Yu rooted people out completely [?]; the calamities of Huai and Heng extended to every last associate [?]. He seemed anxiously intent on exhausting the people’s goodwill. Thus, although he expressed remorse at Luntai, it was sheer good fortune that his state survived. From this we may say: there were outward signs of disaster…

丹書之戒乎拒甘露頌歌之獻則曰凡人
懼則戒心常存喜則侈心易縱聞災而懼
或皆蒙休見瑞而喜或皆致咎斯意也其
何待於旅獒之訓乎定賦節用以安民生
崇本祛末以紓國計其
諭於太史令起居注者詳矣
乘輿服御皆以銅代宮室絺構一以樸素其
諭於中書省有司者明矣以欽恤二字爲用
刑之本
punctuated:
無災之實，不害其為休徵；有祥之文，無祥之實，不害其為咎徵。其理益以明矣。
洪惟我太祖高皇帝奮起布衣，登臨大寶，畏天戒而晝曝於日、夜卧於地，悲人窮而軫其饑寒、恤其老幼。講《洪範》庶徵之應，則曰：「天道微妙難知，人事感通易見。修德則災害不生，不修德則災異疊見。」斯言也，其何由於《丹書》之戒乎？拒甘露頌歌之獻，則曰：「凡人懼則戒心常存，喜則侈心易縱。聞災而懼，或皆蒙休；見瑞而喜，或皆致咎。」斯意也，其何待於《旅獒》之訓乎？定賦節用，以安民生；崇本祛末，以紓國計。其諭於太史令、起居注者詳矣。乘輿服御，皆以銅代；宫室締構，一以朴素。其諭於中書省有司者明矣。以欽恤二字為用刑之本，
translation_en:
…yet without the reality of calamity, this does not prevent it from being an auspicious sign; when there is the outward appearance of good fortune but no actual good fortune, this does not prevent it from being an ominous sign. The principle thus becomes still clearer.
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao rose from the common people and ascended the imperial throne. In awe of Heaven’s warnings, he exposed himself to the sun by day and lay upon the ground at night. Grieving over the people’s distress, he took their hunger and cold to heart and cared for their aged and young. Discussing the responses manifested in the various signs described in the “Great Plan” (Hongfan), he said: “The Way of Heaven is subtle and difficult to know; the sympathetic responses elicited by human affairs are easy to see. If one cultivates virtue, calamities do not arise; if one fails to cultivate virtue, calamities and anomalies appear repeatedly.” How could these words have depended upon the admonitions of the Cinnabar Writing (Danshu)? When he rejected the presentation of songs celebrating sweet dew, he said: “When people are afraid, a vigilant mind is always present; when they are pleased, an extravagant mind is easily indulged. Those who hear of calamity and become afraid may all receive blessings; those who see auspicious signs and rejoice may all bring misfortune upon themselves.” What need did this intention have of the instructions in “The Hounds of Lü” (Lü Ao)? He fixed taxes and restrained expenditure to secure the people’s livelihood; he promoted the fundamental occupation of agriculture and eliminated subsidiary pursuits to ease the state’s finances. His instructions to the Grand Astrologer and the Imperial Diarist on these matters were detailed. For imperial conveyances and articles of personal use, copper was used as a substitute throughout; in constructing palaces, simplicity was the sole rule. His instructions to the responsible officials of the Secretariat were explicit. He made the two words “reverence” and “compassion” the foundation for administering punishments…

諭諸內外法司亦嚴且切矣
盛德大業高冠百王深仁厚澤培植萬世眞
有以陋成周於不居者矣
列聖相承率循是道及我
皇上天縱聖明
日隆繼述
懋德建中則見於
敬一之箴
===

郊廟之正權倖之革者可徵也諸福之物可致
之祥又
禁天下勿復以
聞頃因
後殿之災斷自
宸衷罷安南之征停沙河之工
詔三大臣審錄繫囚是心也即古帝王之心
也

欽天之記者可誦也脩政導和則見於

之祥又

宸衷罷安南之征停沙河之工
詔三大臣審録繫囚是心也即古帝王之心
也
punctuated:
頒律令二書，革姦吏之弊，其諭諸內外法司亦嚴且切矣。盛德大業，高冠百王；深仁厚澤，培植萬世，眞有以陋成周於不居者矣。
列聖相承，率循是道。及我皇上，天縱聖明，日隆繼述。懋德建中，則見於《敬一》之箴、《欽天》之記者可誦也；脩政導和，則見於郊廟之正、權倖之革者可徵也。諸福之物、可致之祥，又禁天下勿復以聞。頃因後殿之災，斷自宸衷，罷安南之征，停沙河之工，詔三大臣審錄繫囚。是心也，即古帝王之心也，
translation_en:
…He promulgated the two books of statutes and ordinances and abolished the abuses of corrupt clerks. His instructions to judicial offices within and outside the capital were likewise stern and emphatic. His abundant virtue and great achievements surpassed those of all former kings; his profound benevolence and generous bounty nurtured ten thousand generations. Truly, he made even the flourishing Zhou appear inferior, without claiming such greatness for himself.
Successive sage emperors followed one another in adhering to this way. Now our present Emperor, endowed by Heaven with sagely discernment, daily advances the work of carrying forward his predecessors’ achievements. His cultivation of virtue and establishment of the mean can be read in his Admonition on Revering the One (Jingyi) and Record of Revering Heaven (Qintian). His reform of government and promotion of harmony can be verified in his rectification of the suburban and ancestral-temple sacrifices and his removal of powerful favorites. As for objects betokening blessings and auspicious signs that might be brought forth, he further prohibited anyone throughout the realm from reporting them to him. Recently, following the calamity at the rear palace hall, he resolved in his imperial heart to abandon the expedition against Annan and halt the construction works at Shahe. He commanded three high ministers to review the cases of prisoners in custody. This heart is the very heart of the emperors and kings of antiquity…

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
祖宗列聖之心也而豈漢文可同日語哉一時
臣民歌舞載道
宗社億萬年無疆之休端在是矣而執事乃欲
問道於盲有
君如此其忍負之毋亦至情之不能已耳夫君
代天以理物者也臣承君以行令者也故
元首明則股肱良而庶事康股肱喜則元
首起而百工煕交相成者也伏願
聖天子終始一德常以
===
天之心為心賢公卿精白一心咸以
上之憂為憂安南固罷也而宣大之擾陝西三
鎮之患密雲遼東之時警其將何以禦之
沙河固停也而諸工之興竹木磚瓦之取
物料百需之徵派其將何以已之
京師之繫囚固審錄也而天下之大一夫積
忿一婦含寃亦不敢謂其盡無也又將何
以矜之癢疴疾痛舉切于身經營節省一
如其家有所謂可而有否焉則獻其否以

punctuated: 祖宗列聖之心也，而豈漢文可同日語哉？一時臣民歌舞載道，宗社億萬年無疆之休，端在是矣。而執事乃欲問道於盲，有君如此，其忍負之？毋亦至情之不能已耳。夫君代天以理物者也，臣承君以行令者也。故元首明則股肱良而庶事康，股肱喜則元首起而百工煕，交相成者也。伏願聖天子終始一德，常以天之心為心；賢公卿精白一心，咸以上之憂為憂。安南固罷也，而宣大之擾、陝西三鎮之患、密雲遼東之時警，其將何以禦之？沙河固停也，而諸工之興、竹木磚瓦之取、物料百需之徵派，其將何以已之？京師之繫囚固審錄也，而天下之大，一夫積忿、一婦含寃，亦不敢謂其盡無也，又將何以矜之？癢疴疾痛，舉切于身；經營節省，一如其家。有所謂可而有否焉，則獻其否以
translation_en:
…and the heart of the illustrious ancestral emperors. How could Emperor Wen of Han be spoken of in the same breath? For a time, officials and commoners filled the roads with song and dance. Here indeed lies the source of boundless blessings for the imperial ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain for countless ages. Yet you, honored examiners, would ask a blind man the way. With such a ruler, how could one bear to fail him? Perhaps it is simply that the deepest feelings cannot be restrained.

The ruler governs all things on Heaven’s behalf; ministers serve the ruler by carrying out his commands. Thus, when the head is enlightened, the limbs are worthy and all affairs prosper; when the limbs rejoice, the head rises to action and the hundred offices flourish. Each brings the other to fulfillment. I humbly wish that the sagely Son of Heaven remain constant in virtue from beginning to end, always taking Heaven’s heart as his own, and that the worthy dukes and ministers purify their hearts and unite in purpose, all taking their sovereign’s concerns as their own.

The expedition against Annan has indeed been abandoned; but how will the disturbances in Xuanfu and Datong, the troubles of the three garrisons in Shaanxi, and the recurrent alarms in Miyun and Liaodong be resisted? The works at Shahe have indeed been halted; but how will the launching of other construction projects, the procurement of bamboo, timber, bricks, and tiles, and the levies and requisitions for materials and innumerable other needs be stopped? The cases of prisoners in the capital have indeed been reviewed; but in so vast a realm, one dare not say that there is no man nursing resentment or woman suffering an unredressed wrong. How, then, will compassion be shown to them?

Every itch, ailment, and pain should be felt as keenly as if in one’s own body; management and economy should be practiced just as in one’s own household. When something deemed acceptable contains something unacceptable, one should present its unacceptable aspects in order to…

title: 嘉靖十六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
成其可有所謂否而有可焉則獻其可以
去其否都俞吁咈眞若堯舜禹臯交會于
一堂迪畏棐恭眞若文武周召相際于一
時恤煢獨釋逋負薄稅斂務有以厚之而
不困蠲煩苛黜貪酷時工作務有以生之
而不傷雪寃抑議功能省刑罰務有以通
其情而不盡如是則政何有不善民何有
不安而天變何有不弭也哉若夫百祥日
降四靈畢至此固體信達順之道然有之
靡益無之靡補亦豈有識者之樂道哉孟
子曰欲爲君盡君道欲爲臣盡臣道二者
皆法堯舜而已矣不以舜之所以事堯事
君不敬其君者也不以堯之所以治民治
民賊其民者也愚也敢誦斯言以爲今日
之
君相獻
第四問
徐燦
